This study developed and validated an AI-based Hypothetical Learning Trajectory (HLT) framework to foster metacognitive skills among 72 secondary school students over an eight-session adaptive learning intervention. Drawing on Flavell's (1979) metacognitive theory and Simon's (2020) HLT model, the research employed K-Means clustering to identify distinct learner profiles based on twelve behavioral and metacognitive features extracted from a digital learning platform. Clustering analysis revealed three meaningful profiles: low metacognitive (33%), moderate metacognitive (39%), and high metacognitive (28% of students). These profiles were then translated into differentiated HLT pathways—structured scaffolding for low learners, monitoring feedback with strategy adjustment for moderate learners, and self-directed inquiry with meta-evaluation for high learners. Longitudinal assessment measured metacognitive gains across eight sessions using pre-post comparisons and learning rate analysis. Results demonstrated that all clusters improved significantly, with low metacognitive learners showing the largest relative gain (88% performance increase) and moderate learners achieving the largest absolute gain (+35 points). However, the achievement gap between low and high groups persisted, confirming Stanovich's (1986) Matthew effect in metacognitive development. PCA revealed that a single latent component explained 92.8% of behavioral variance, indicating that metacognitive competence functions as a unified continuum in digital trace data. This study developed and validated an AI-based Hypothetical Learning Trajectory (HLT) framework to foster metacognitive skills among 72 secondary school students over an eight-session adaptive learning intervention. Drawing on Flavell's (1979) metacognitive theory and Simon's (2020) HLT model, the research employed K-Means clustering to identify distinct learner profiles based on twelve behavioral and metacognitive features extracted from a digital learning platform. Clustering analysis revealed three meaningful profiles: low metacognitive (33%), moderate metacognitive (39%), and high metacognitive (28% of students). These profiles were then translated into differentiated HLT pathways—structured scaffolding for low learners, monitoring feedback with strategy adjustment for moderate learners, and self-directed inquiry with meta-evaluation for high learners. Longitudinal assessment measured metacognitive gains across eight sessions using pre-post comparisons and learning rate analysis. Results demonstrated that all clusters improved significantly, with low metacognitive learners showing the largest relative gain (88% performance increase) and moderate learners achieving the largest absolute gain (+35 points). However, the achievement gap between low and high groups persisted, confirming Stanovich's (1986) Matthew effect in metacognitive development. PCA revealed that a single latent component explained 92.8% of behavioral variance, indicating that metacognitive competence functions as a unified continuum in digital trace data. The study contributes empirical validation that clustering-derived HLT pathways can be successfully operationalized within AI-mediated adaptive systems. Implications for instructional design, AI system development, and educational policy are discussed, alongside limitations regarding sample size, control group absence, and measurement validity.

6.2 Limitations
The sample size of 72 students, while adequate for exploratory clustering, is relatively small for establishing stable solutions that generalize across populations. As Chander and Gopalakrishnan (
2023
) noted, clustering results can be sensitive to sample composition; replication with larger samples (N = 200–300) is necessary. The sample was drawn from a single educational context; metacognitive behaviors may manifest differently across subjects, age groups, and cultural contexts. Additionally, as Alzahrani et al. (
2025
) cautioned, clustering effectiveness depends on feature selection; different feature sets might produce different cluster structures.
The absence of a control group means observed improvements cannot be causally attributed to the AI-HLT intervention rather than practice effects or natural maturation. Essa et al. (
2023
) identified this as a common limitation in adaptive learning research. The synthetic data generation for certain analyses may underestimate within-cluster variability and overestimate the smoothness of improvement curves. Furthermore, as Walker et al. (
2025
) critically noted, algorithm transparency remains a challenge; the clustering and HLT assignment algorithms operate as black boxes, and whether users would trust or appropriately override system recommendations was not empirically investigated.
The operationalization of metacognition through digital trace behaviors captures only observable actions that may be imperfect proxies for internal processes. As Flavell (
1979
) originally conceptualized metacognition as primarily internal, this measurement gap cannot be fully resolved through behavioral data alone. The eight-session duration cannot address long-term retention or transfer of metacognitive skills. Michalsky (
2021
) emphasized that metacognitive development requires extended time horizons. Finally, reliance on platform-specific traces raises questions about measurement equivalence across different learning systems. Future research should prioritize multi-platform replication, longer interventions (16–24 sessions), and multi-method assessment approaches combining trace data with think-aloud protocols or validated questionnaires.
Funding Statement
This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.
Conflict of Interest Statement
The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Author Contributions
Gunawan contributed to the conceptualization, theoretical framework development, and overall coordination of the research. Mikrayanti were responsible for methodology development, research instrument design, and data collection. Lala Intan Komalasari conducted data analysis, validation procedures, and interpretation of the findings. All authors reviewed and approved the final version of the manuscript and contributed to its scholarly development.
Ethical Approval
This study received ethical approval from the Research Ethics Committee, Nggusuwaru Bima University, Indonesia. All research procedures involving human participants were conducted in accordance with relevant ethical guidelines and regulations, including the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Ethical approval was granted under approval number 012/UNSWA/I/2026, dated January 5, 2025.
Consent to Participate
Informed consent was obtained from all participants involved in this study. For participants under the age of 18, written consent was obtained from their parents and/or legal guardians.
Consent to Publish
Not applicable.
Data Availability Statement
Data supporting this study's findings available upon request.
Clinical Trial Registration
Not applicable.
